title: Markdown Garden
summary: A tiny notebook for ideas, components, and sketchy experiments.
content: This garden is where small interface thoughts get planted before they become full projects.
The useful part is not the markdown itself. It is the rhythm around it: quick notes, durable tags, and a layout that makes old ideas easy to rediscover.
I keep the surface soft because writing tools should invite revision instead of feeling like a control room.

title: Soft UI Field Notes
summary: How rounded panels, pencil lines, and warm spacing keep pages friendly.
content: A soft interface still needs structure. The trick is to keep the grid disciplined while letting borders, shadows, and spacing feel handmade.
I use a small token set first: paper, ink, muted text, line color, and three accent families. Once those are stable, the rest of the page can vary without becoming random.
The best detail here is restraint. A little wobble in an icon is charming. Too much wobble makes the interface harder to scan.

title: Presence Notes
summary: Making little status widgets feel alive without making them noisy.
content: Presence UI is most useful when it gives a page a pulse without demanding attention.
A changing bpm number, currently editing label, and viewer count are enough to imply activity. They do not need to be exact to make the interface feel current.
For real systems, this layer would connect to a websocket or server event stream. For this page, local state keeps the behavior lightweight.

title: Relations Demo Kitchen
summary: A small content graph for testing tags, references, and directory links.
content: A demo kitchen is a place for intentionally tiny examples. It should be small enough that broken relationships are obvious.
The content graph starts with tags, then gains references, backlinks, and directory-like groupings only when those relationships answer a real navigation question.
This keeps the implementation honest: if a link model is confusing in a toy dataset, it will be worse in production.

title: Cute Buttons Audit
summary: A practical pass over hover states, focus rings, and friendly affordances.
content: Cute buttons still need to behave like buttons. They need clear hit areas, focus states, disabled states, and labels that do not collapse on mobile.
The hand-drawn style works because the shape language is consistent: rounded corners, thin ink borders, soft fill, and a tiny lift on hover.
Accessibility is part of the style here. A button that is pleasant but vague is unfinished.

title: Tiny Frontend Almanac
summary: Things I keep relearning about responsive grids and readable type.
content: Every frontend almanac eventually says the same thing: stable spacing beats clever layouts.
Readable pages come from constraints. Use max widths, predictable grids, and typography that does not scale wildly just because the viewport changed.
The page should feel composed at desktop size and still deliberate when collapsed to a single column.
